http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/power.text: At least 111 people were killed and hundreds of buildings damaged after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, the country's President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday.De la Espriella said that at least 87 people had been injured and that he had declared a state of emergency.“You are not alone. The state is present and taking action,” he said.The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogotá.The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, the US Geological Survey and Colombia’s counterpart reported.The USGS said it struck at a depth of 107 kilometers and was also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.The quake left cities across the west of the country ravaged.A mix of residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid concerns by authorities of aftershocks.Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit.Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors.“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”Colombia's Geological Service said on Monday that it had been “the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira.The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people.At the same time the quake brought down buildings in Colombia, desperate families in Venezuela continued to search the ruins for the bodies of their loved ones.In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings.”In nearby Manizales, a city nestled in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Jorge Eduardo Rojas, the mayor of Manizales said two people had died in the city “because of the quake” and asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks.Authorities in the rural state of Choco, the epicentre of the quake, reported injured people and damaged buildings in the capital, but provided few details.In Cali, a city 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed.Small earthquakes, known as “temblores,” are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare.In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia, killed more than 1,100 people.

https://www.foxnews.com/politics/us-ally.text: Russia’s threat of "consequences" against Britain and a stark warning from a senior Polish defense official are intensifying concerns that Moscow could seek to test NATO directly as the war in Ukraine continues. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said his country is actively preparing for the possibility of conflict, telling Super Express in an interview published Aug. 17: "We are preparing for war, hoping that it never happens." The Polish Embassy in Washington told Fox News Digital that Warsaw’s accelerated defense preparations are intended to deter potential aggression rather than signal that conflict is inevitable. RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS The embassy pointed to Poland’s defense spending of nearly 5% of GDP and invoked the Latin principle Si vis pacem, para bellum — "If you want peace, prepare for war" — saying that, given Russia’s war in Ukraine and what Poland views as Moscow’s imperial ambitions, strengthening deterrence is the country’s only sound strategy. A European diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, backed Tomczyk and said Poland sees a pattern of escalating Russian pressure on multiple fronts. "We are hurrying to be prepared for war since Russia is giving us and our neighbors constant signals that they want us back as their vassals, their colonial backyard," the diplomat told Fox News Digital. The diplomat pointed to what they described as Russian disinformation campaigns, cyberattacks, sabotage efforts and repeated tests of Poland’s air defenses, as well as increasingly frequent nuclear rhetoric from Russian officials and propagandists. "Altogether, it shows quite clearly that if Russia or Belarus saw any chance to attack Poland to destroy an obstacle to restoring the Soviet or Tsarist Russian empire in Eastern Europe, they would do it without hesitation," the diplomat said. The diplomat added that Tomczyk therefore had "quite solid bases to state his prediction," while stressing that the concern was not rooted in hostility toward ordinary Russians. "We want to have Russia as a good neighbor, business partner. We would like to host their tourists. We want to have a cultural exchange with them," the diplomat said. "But they — at least the imperialists who are the foundation of the Putin administration — would like to turn Poland, the Baltics and, of course, Ukraine back into their colonial part of Europe." UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Retired Air Force Gen. Philip Breedlove, who commanded U.S. European Command and served as NATO’s supreme allied commander Europe from 2013 to 2016, told Fox News Digital that Poland's warning reflects a concern shared by many former military leaders. "It’s a problem that many of us are worried about," Breedlove said. "They’re trying to test the alliance: Is Italy going to go to war? Is Spain going to go to war? There are several places where Russia could try to snatch something. Their goal is to divide and ultimately break up the alliance." Breedlove warned Moscow could attempt a provocation calibrated to create uncertainty over whether NATO should respond collectively. "It is likely that Russia will try to initiate a provocation that is just enough to raise the question of a NATO response," he said, arguing that Moscow’s objective would be to expose divisions among allies. NATO’s Article 4 allows members to request consultations when an ally’s territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened. Article 5 provides for collective defense following an armed attack, although NATO says Article 4 consultations are not a prerequisite for action under Article 5. The comments follow similar warnings from other eastern-flank governments. The Associated Press reported July 15 that Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said intelligence pointed to possible limited Russian attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltics or Poland. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Warsaw was preparing "very intensively for various scenarios," according to AP. Russia rejected the allegations. RUSSIA LINKED TO ARSON ATTACKS ON PROPERTIES CONNECTED TO UK PM KEIR STARMER, POLICE SAY The warnings came as tensions between Moscow and London escalated Tuesday. Russia’s embassy in Britain threatened unspecified "consequences" after The Times reported British-made drones had been used by Ukraine for long-range strikes inside Russia, according to Reuters on Aug. 18. Britain’s Ministry of Defense did not confirm whether British drones were used, Reuters reported. "London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer," the Russian Embassy said. The British defense ministry responded that Britain stood "shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine," according to Reuters. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov escalated the rhetoric later Tuesday, saying Moscow had the right to regard direct British involvement in strikes on Russian territory as participation in the war, according to Reuters on Aug. 18. Separately, Russian state television host Vladimir Solovyov called for using Russia’s Poseidon weapon against Britain, saying: "Give the British three days to learn to breathe underwater, then hit them with Poseidon," The Times reported Aug. 18. Poseidon is a nuclear-powered, nuclear-capable underwater weapon that Russia said it successfully tested in October 2025, Reuters reported at the time. Breedlove described the rhetoric as part of a broader Russian information campaign aimed at coercing Western governments. US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING "Without question, Russia is fighting an information war and trying to achieve what practitioners call ‘reflexive control’ to try to force NATO capitulation," Breedlove said. He argued that Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy, logistics and defense-industrial targets are creating growing pressure on the Kremlin and said President Vladimir Putin may increasingly seek to portray NATO itself as the external enemy. Breedlove said NATO is capable of facing Russia in a conventional war but warned that the alliance faces a different vulnerability exposed by the conflict in Ukraine. "What NATO is not ready for — and what the U.S. is not ready for — is the new kind of drone warfare that Russia is waging against Ukraine," Breedlove said. "Our air defense capabilities in the West are not even close to what is needed for the level of drone warfare that Russia is waging against Ukraine." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the Russian and British embassies for comment but did not receive responses in time for publication. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

https://www.wiltshiretimes.co.uk/news/26.text: Education Bradford-on-avon Calne Chippenham Corsham Melksham Trowbridge Warminster Wiltshire Wiltshire GCSE students get top grades and record pass rates By Andrea Glennon News Reporter Share 0 Comments 7 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Students across Wiltshire have been celebrating another successful year of GCSE results. While the national pass rate dropped slightly as some 67.3 per cent of entries received a grade 4/C or above, down from 6, schools across the county had much to celebrate. At Malmesbury School, the number of students achieving the strong pass (Grade 5) in English and Maths continued to rise, as did the number of grades at the very top end with 26 per cent of all grades a 7 or higher. St Laurence School in Bradford on Avon celebrated an 83 per cent pass rate in English, and an almost 80 per cent pass rate in maths. The John of Gaunt cohort in Trowbridge reported a higher attainment percentage at each grade boundary for the combined English and mathematics GCSE than the AQA exam board average across all its schools. Students and staff at St Augustine's Catholic College in Trowbridge were pleased to receive their GCSE results, recognising their hard work and achievement across a broad and ambitious curriculum. The Corsham School headteacher Rod Bell was delighted with his pupils’ efforts and said this year’s students had to navigate a very different educational experience owing to the pandemic. Springfields Academy in Corsham celebrated its seventh consecutive year in which all pupils secured a post-16 placement. The school supports young people with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) and saw pupils achieve GCSEs and celebrate success in Functional Skills, Entry Level certificates and vocational qualifications. Staff at Abbeyfield Academy in Chippenham said they "couldn't be prouder" of this year's GCSE cohort. Headteacher Nick Norgrove said: “It was lovely to spend time with students, parents and staff this morning to celebrate their results. At Sheldon School in Chippenham, grades have improved once again as the school continues to perform well above the national average with 74 per cent of GCSE entries achieving grades 9–4 Every student who sat exams in chemistry, Polish, Russian, Chinese, statistics and Bengali achieved a grade 4 or above. Meanwhile headteacher at Hardenhuish School in Chippenham, Lisa Percy, said it was an absolute joy to share in the students’ celebrations. St John’s Marlborough revelled as more than 80 per cent of students achieved a pass in both English and Maths and almost 30 per cent of all grades were at grade 7 or above. Lavington School in Devizes saw a pass rate of over 80 per cent in both English and Maths and 20 per cent of all grades 7 and above. Students from Devizes School were delighted by a fantastic set of smiling faces, individual success stories and overall results for the school. Kingdown School in Warminster celebrated a strong set of GCSE and Vocational results. Headteacher Shelley Tuke said: "It has been fantastic to welcome them into school this morning and see so many extremely happy students celebrating their results with their friends, families and teachers. Students from Melksham Oak praised its students for a GCSE results day success. Standout results included Jessica Jones who achieved seven grade 9s and two grade 8s and is staying at Melksham Oak Sixth Form to pursue Sciences. At St Mary’s Calne, 56 per cent of GCSEs taken were awarded grade 8 or 9, with more than a third (31 per cent) achieving the top grade of 9. In total, 79 per cent of all grades were 9-7 and 37 per cent of pupils achieved at least nine grades at 9-7. http://www.euronews.com/2026/09/09/us-de.text: US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days, as Iran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan.US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the crews of all five vessels — the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya — were warned to abandon ship before the strikes.The targeted warship evaded both Iranian attacks without casualties, CENTCOM said.Iranian state-affiliated news agency confirmed one oil tanker was struck near Jask and another tanker four miles off Kharg Island. Iran's state broadcaster has reported that a commercial vessel was also attacked in the coastal waters of Jask county.According to Tasnim, citing local sources, the attack on the tanker near Kharg caused no casualties.Iran launched missiles at US targets in Jordan following the tanker strikes, according to Iranian state-run television."Given the malign actions of the terrorist US military in targeting several oil tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the area of the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which host these terrorists and are partners in their aggression, to leave their vessels immediately, whether at anchorage or at the quays, as they will be targeted," IRGC said.The Khatam al-Anbiya central command followed with a threat to US bases in the region."The US military has ordered Iranian oil tankers to evacuate so that it can strike them; therefore I declare that any attack on Iranian oil tankers will result in US bases in the region being targeted by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Major General Abdollahi said in a statement.Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and that two others landed in uninhabited areas. No casualties were reported.Jordan hosts several US military installations and has been a repeated target of Iranian strikes since the war began on 28 February.Iran also said it had captured a US unmanned underwater vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz before dawn, broadcasting images of what it described as the captured drone on state television. Iran had claimed to have struck a US Navy sea drone on Sunday.The Trump administration separately announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo providers, in a further effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.The exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations since the framework deal the two sides signed in June broke down the following month.Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.The US has been enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports while Tehran has sought to impose its own transit regime on commercial shipping through the strait.

https://www.dw.com/en/serbia-election-ca.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OdWU Voters cast their ballots at a polling station in Belgrade in Serbia's closely contested parliamentary election Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS Advertisement Polls have closed in Serbia's closely contested Sunday election that could bring an end to more than a decade of rule by long-time leader Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). Pre-election polls suggested a tight race between the SNS and the newly formed, youth-backed Students' List, which emerged from a mass student protest movement. Turnout was on course to be the highest since 1993. What is Serbia's student protest movement The protests were sparked by the deadly collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi ‌Sad in 2024. The disaster killed 16 people and stirred widespread anger over alleged corruption, poor construction standards and a lack of accountability for public infrastructure projects. Protesters accused the government of allowing corruption and political patronage to undermine public safety, allegations the authorities have rejected. Demonstrations demanding accountability have since snowballed into Serbia's largest movement since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What began with university students staging blockades and marches soon drew support from teachers, farmers and other sections of Serbian society, turning a demand for justice over the disaster into a broader challenge to Vucic's grip on power. Vucic faces tough election challenge SNS won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics ever since. Vucic himself first came to power as prime minister in 2014 before becoming president in 2017. After calling snap elections last month, Vucic stepped down as president to run for prime minister. Under Serbia's constitution, Vucic cannot run for a third presidential term Image: Jelena Djukic Pejic/DW His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia's constitution prevents him from serving a third term. Critics have accused him of concentrating power, undermining independent media and weakening democratic institutions. He and his party deny the allegations. The student movement has sought to channel the energy of the street protests into an electoral challenge, presenting itself as an alternative to both the ruling party and Serbia's established opposition. Highest voter turnout By 1 p.m. (1200 GMT), 41.1% of eligible voters had cast their ballots, up from 26.6% at the same stage in the December 2023 parliamentary election, according to independent election monitor CRTA. And then by 6:00 p.m. (1700 GMT), two hours before polls were set to close, "64.89 percent out of the total" voters had cast their ballots, Serbia's Statistics Office director Branko Josipovic said in a press conference. After voting at a kindergarten on the outskirts of Belgrade, Vucic said he hoped the election would proceed smoothly. "We will heed the democratic will of the citizens. You can win or lose an election. Either way, we will act responsibly," said Vucic, who is seeking to become prime minister. Cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic heads the Students' List but is neither the movement's leader nor its designated candidate for prime minister. "I hope that today will pass in a democratic atmosphere, in peace, and that we will legitimately elect a new government in Serbia," he said after casting his ballot in Novi Sad. The election is being closely watched in Europe. Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, but its accession process has been hampered by concerns over democratic standards and the rule of law. Vucic has also maintained close ties with Russia and refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine. The vote comes six months after Peter Magyar's victory in Hungary , when he defeated Vucic's ally, Viktor Orban . Polling stations close at 8 p.m. local time (1900 GMT). Serbia's student revolt: Will it bring about change? Narrowing margins suggest a shifting political landscape and growing momentum for anti-government protests.
